summary: Tanzania lies in East Africa and was formed in 1964 by the merger of Tanganyika and Zanzibar; it is home to Mount Kilimanjaro and Serengeti National Park.

ranking.name: Christianity
ranking.description: In the mid-19th century European missionaries began penetrating the East African interior, and in 1868 the Catholic Holy Ghost Fathers set up a mission station at Bagamoyo to shelter rescued slaves. During the period of German East Africa (1885-1919), German Lutherans, the Moravian Church and Catholics founded schools and hospitals in the interior; after the British took over as mandatory power, Anglicans and other denominations also expanded. Because mission schools were the main source of modern education, Christianity became widespread in the mainland interior and highlands, and the first president, Nyerere, was also a devout Catholic.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Islam reached the East African coast in the 8th-10th centuries with Arab and Persian traders, and Swahili city-states such as Kilwa became Muslim trading centers. In the 19th century the Omani sultan Sayyid Said moved his capital to Zanzibar, and Arab and Swahili caravans followed the ivory and slave trade routes into the interior, bringing Islam to places such as Tabora and Ujiji. As a result, Muslims today are concentrated along the coast and on Zanzibar, which is almost entirely Muslim.

ranking.name: Traditional beliefs
ranking.description: The more than one hundred ethnic groups of Tanzania each originally had their own ancestor worship and belief in nature spirits. Since the 20th century Christianity and Islam have expanded rapidly and most people have converted to one of the two major religions, but many traditional rituals, healers and ancestor-honoring customs still coexist with the new religions, so only a very small number of people follow mainly traditional beliefs.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: Tanzanian society is strongly religious, and religion is closely tied to family and community life; very few people state clearly that they have no religion. Although Nyerere pursued socialism, he did not suppress religion but instead stressed religious harmony and national unity, so no large-scale secularization occurred.

religion.background: Tanzania's coast has traded with Arabs, Persians and Indians since the 8th century, and Islam took root in the Swahili city-states; in the 19th century the Omani sultan established a center of rule in Zanzibar, and caravans carried Islam into the interior. During the same period European missionaries began spreading Christianity, and mission schools expanded rapidly under German and British colonial rule. In 1964 Tanganyika and Zanzibar merged to form Tanzania, and Nyerere's government stressed religious harmony; Christianity and Islam have coexisted largely peacefully ever since.

language.official: Swahili and English are the official languages.

ranking.name: Swahili
ranking.description: Swahili is a Bantu language that formed through exchanges between the East African coast and Arab and Persian traders from the first millennium onward, and it absorbed a great deal of Arabic vocabulary. In the 19th century it became the common language of inland trade along the caravan routes, and the German colonial government also used Swahili as an administrative language. After independence in 1961 Nyerere made it the national language and promoted it throughout primary education, government and the media in order to unite the more than one hundred ethnic groups, so that over 90 percent of citizens can use it.

ranking.name: English
ranking.description: English's status derives from British mandate and trusteeship rule over Tanganyika from 1919 to 1961, when it was the language of the colonial government, the courts and education from secondary school upward. After independence English remained an official language, used in higher education, the judiciary and international business; however, most people speak Swahili or their own ethnic language as a mother tongue, and English is only a second or third language.

language.history: More than one hundred languages are spoken in Tanzania, most belonging to the Bantu family, with some Nilotic, Cushitic and Sandawe languages as well. Swahili formed in the trading city-states of the East African coast, was first written in the Arabic script, and switched to the Latin alphabet after the 19th century. During the German colonial period Swahili was used for administration, while the British period promoted English-language education. After independence in 1961, Nyerere vigorously promoted Swahili, making Tanzania one of the few African countries successfully unified by an indigenous language.

ranking.name: Ugali
ranking.description: A thick porridge made by boiling white maize flour in water, kneaded into a mass; one pinches off a small ball by hand and dips it in stew, beans or greens, and it has a firm texture.
ranking.history: Maize originated in the Americas and was brought to East Africa by the Portuguese after the 16th century; during the colonial period in the 20th century it was widely promoted to supply labor for mines and plantations and gradually replaced traditional millet and sorghum. In the 1960s and 1970s, when Nyerere carried out his collectivization policy of "Ujamaa," maize became a focus of national food policy. Today ugali is the everyday staple of nearly every Tanzanian household and also symbolizes the shared food culture of East Africa.

ranking.name: Nyama choma (grilled meat)
ranking.description: Goat or beef seasoned with salt and slow-grilled over charcoal, cut into pieces and eaten with the tomato and onion salad "kachumbari" and ugali.
ranking.history: "Nyama choma" means "grilled meat" in Swahili and comes from the tradition of East African cattle-herding peoples of roasting meat over charcoal; nomadic peoples such as the Maasai still live by herding today. In the cities of Tanzania and Kenya, going to a bar or grill house on weekends to order grilled goat with beer is an important social activity for gatherings of friends and celebrations. Nyama choma is usually priced by weight and everyone sits around sharing it, reflecting East Africa's culture of valuing sharing.

ranking.name: Chips mayai (French fry omelette)
ranking.description: Freshly fried french fries are put in a frying pan and cooked with beaten eggs poured over them into a thick omelette, eaten with tomato chili sauce or a tomato and onion salad.
ranking.history: Chips mayai is a relatively new street snack, generally believed to have appeared among street vendors in Dar es Salaam in the late 20th century; its name combines the English "chips" with the Swahili "mayai" (eggs). It is cheap and simple to make, and quickly became a popular dinner for students and office workers. Today it has become a representative food of Tanzanian urban life and can be seen at roadside stalls across the country in the evenings.

ranking.name: Pilau
ranking.description: A spiced rice dish in which cumin, cardamom, cloves, cinnamon and black pepper are fried until fragrant, then rice and beef or chicken are added and simmered; it is golden in color and richly aromatic.
ranking.history: Pilau derives from the Middle Eastern and Indian "pilaf" and came to the East African coast across the Indian Ocean with Arab, Persian and Indian traders. In the 19th century the Omani sultans planted cloves on a large scale in Zanzibar, making it the world's largest clove producer, and spices thus became a hallmark of Swahili cooking. At weddings, Eid al-Fitr and family gatherings, pilau is the most popular main dish, often served with a tomato and onion salad.

ranking.name: Mandazi
ranking.description: Dough kneaded from flour, sugar, coconut milk and cardamom is cut into triangles and deep-fried; the outside is golden, the inside fluffy, with a light sweetness.
ranking.history: Mandazi originated on the Swahili coast; the use of coconut milk and cardamom reflects the influence of Arab and Indian Ocean trade, and it later spread to the East African interior along trade routes. In Tanzania it is a classic snack served with milk tea at breakfast and teatime, and street vendors and housewives fry and sell it every morning at dawn. During Ramadan, mandazi are also a common treat on the iftar table.
